Paragraph:
Translation: One who is, however, taking pleasure in the self, who is illumined in the self, who rejoices in and is satisfied with the self only, fully satiated—for him there is no duty.

Purport (Excerpt): A person who is fully Krsna conscious, and is fully satisfied by his acts in Krsna consciousness, no longer has any duty to perform... all impiety within is instantly cleansed... His duty thus becomes self-illuminated by the grace of the Lord... no longer interested in material activities...
Situation/Problem_Faced: Understanding the state of complete internal self-sufficiency where external social mandates no longer apply as obligations.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Krishna describes the enlightened state: one who finds total joy, illumination, and contentment within the true Self is free from external obligations because their heart is already purified.
Outcome/Resolution: Arjuna learns that the ultimate goal of all prescribed duties is total internal fulfillment and self-realization.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Self-Actualization: Achieving complete psychological and spiritual fulfillment from within
Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Internal Validation: Finding contentment independently of external approval or material circumstances
Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Emotional Independence: Reaching a state of complete emotional security and self-sufficiency

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Atma-rati / Atma-tripta (Rejoicing in and satisfied with the true Self)
Karya na vidyate (Having no compulsory duties left to perform)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: For a soul who has attained complete inner satisfaction in God consciousness, formal social and ritual duties are no longer compulsory. Such a person's inner purity and self-realization place them beyond external mandates.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: True peace occurs when your sense of self-worth is internally grounded rather than dependent on external validation, status, or material acquisition. Self-actualized individuals operate out of wholeness rather than needy obligation.
